output.data:
Does gut lymphoid tissue sit in its own spatial domain?

Gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) aggregates immune and stromal cells into compact follicles that look unlike the surrounding lamina propria on a tissue section. If local neighborhoods carry biology, GALT patches should separate from villus epithelium on a map of cell-type context—not only on a manual layer label. We use one ileum slice from Xu et al., 2026 (MERFISH, 30,332 cells). calculate_niche_neighborhood (Palla et al., 2021) builds a spatial graph, summarizes the cell-type mix around each cell, and clusters those summaries with Leiden—like grouping street blocks by who lives next door, not by a single landmark. Following Liu and Li, 2026, we call those computed regional clusters spatial domains in the text below (column names stay niche_k*). We sweep k in 8, 16, and 64 nearest neighbors so you can compare tight crypt-scale domains to villus-scale smoothing. Leiden resolution 0.3 with n_neighbors=15 keeps niche_k8 at 56 domains, niche_k16 at 23, and niche_k64 at 24 on this slice. Open the map, color by niche_k64, then try niche_k8. The default composition plot uses three polygons, one per GALT patch on this section; draw your own lassos to compare other regions. Caveat: a different k or 0.3 resolution can split one anatomical region across several domain IDs. If labels look too fragmented, raise k or lower the resolution; if GALT melts into the lamina propria, lower k.
